subject: Medicine
summary: Hyponatraemia is a common electrolyte disorder where serum sodium falls below 135 mmol/L, often due to water retention or sodium loss. Clinicians must assess volume status, identify the underlying cause, and treat carefully to avoid rapid shifts.

sections.p: Hyponatraemia is defined as a serum sodium concentration <135 mmol/L. Diagnosis requires confirming hypotonicity (low serum osmolality) and ruling out pseudohyponatraemia.
b: Serum sodium <135 mmol/L
Serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg in SIADH

t.b: Low serum osmolality confirms true hyponatraemia; normal or high osmolality suggests pseudohyponatraemia.
High urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg) indicates inappropriate ADH action or renal salt loss.
Urine Na >40 mmol/L suggests renal loss; <20 mmol/L points to extrarenal loss.

sections.p: Severity is staged by serum sodium level and clinical symptoms, guiding urgency of treatment.
b: Mild: 130–134 mmol/L, asymptomatic
Moderate: 125–129 mmol/L, nausea, confusion
Severe: <125 mmol/L, seizures, coma

t.b: Severe hyponatraemia requires urgent correction.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by volume status and ADH activity. In low-resource settings, infections and herbal remedies are common.
b: Hypervolemic: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome

sections.p: Symptoms range from mild nausea to life-threatening seizures, depending on rate and severity of sodium decline.
b: Chronic: muscle cramps, irritability

sections.p: Lab tests guide diagnosis and management. Use the table to decide what to do when tests are unavailable.

t.b: Low osmolality confirms true hyponatraemia.
High urine osmolality suggests SIADH or renal salt loss.
High urine Na indicates renal loss; low indicates extrarenal loss.
Low cortisol with hyponatraemia suggests Addison’s.
Elevated TSH indicates hypothyroidism.
Findings guide SIADH or infection causes.

sections.p: Rapid correction or severe hyponatraemia can cause osmotic demyelination or seizures.
b: Cardiac arrhythmia in severe cases

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neurological symptoms (seizures, coma), rapid drop in sodium, or any sign of impending osmotic demyelination

faq.q: What is the most common cause of hyponatraemia in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Infections such as tuberculosis, malaria, and HIV, often combined with diuretic use or herbal remedies.

faq.q: Why is urine osmolality high in SIADH despite low serum sodium?
faq.a: ADH causes the kidneys to concentrate urine, so urine remains hyperosmolar even when serum is dilute.

faq.q: Can hypertonic saline be used in all patients?
faq.a: Only in symptomatic or severe hyponatraemia; it must be given slowly to avoid overcorrection.

exam: A 68‑year‑old man presents with confusion and a serum sodium of 118 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis and first step in management?
A patient with SIADH is on fluid restriction but remains hyponatraemic. Which drug can be added to correct sodium?
Explain why rapid correction of hyponatraemia can lead to neurological injury.
related: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam reveal volume status, chronicity and possible aetiologies of hyponatraemia, especially in low‑resource settings where laboratory support may be limited.
b: Onset of symptoms – acute (<48 h) vs chronic (>48 h).
Rate of sodium fall – sudden change in fluid intake, diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea.
Medication review – thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine, antipsychotics, herbal diuretics.
Fluid intake – excess water, tea, broth, IV fluids, enteral feeds.
Associated symptoms – nausea, headache, seizures, lethargy, muscle cramps.
Volume cues – oedema, ascites, peripheral oedema, orthostatic symptoms.
Recent surgery, trauma, burns, CNS injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Co‑morbidities – heart failure, cirrhosis, CKD, pregnancy, HIV/TB.

t.b: Look for skin turgor, mucous membranes, facial puffiness, peripheral oedema; positive signs suggest hypervolemia or hypovolemia, but cannot quantify fluid compartments.
Measure supine and standing BP/HR; a fall ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic with tachycardia indicates hypovolaemia; normal orthostatics suggest euvolaemia or hypervolaemia.
Visible jugular pulsation >3 cm above sternal angle indicates raised central venous pressure, supporting hypervolemia; absent JVP does not rule out early heart failure.
Patient supine, percuss flanks; fluid shifts to dependent side becoming dull, upper flank resonant; positive test indicates ascites (hypervolemic state). Cannot differentiate cause of ascites.
Pitting edema graded 1+ to 4+; presence supports hypervolemia, but may be absent in early heart failure or cirrhosis.
Glasgow Coma Scale, focal deficits, seizures; severe hyponatraemia may show altered mental status. Bedside test cannot determine chronicity.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Targeted labs differentiate hypo‑, eu‑ and hypervolemic hyponatraemia and identify SIADH, renal loss or adrenal insufficiency, even when some tests are unavailable.
b: Serum sodium <135 mmol/L confirms hyponatraemia.
Serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg defines true hypotonic hyponatraemia.
Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg indicates impaired water excretion (SIADH, hypovolaemia, hypervolemia).
Urine sodium >30 mmol/L with euvolemia suggests SIADH or renal salt loss.
Serum potassium, creatinine, urea help assess renal function and volume status.
Random cortisol >550 nmol/L rules out adrenal crisis; low cortisol with ACTH stimulation blunted response confirms primary adrenal insufficiency.
Thyroid‑stimulating hormone (TSH) normal excludes hypothyroidism as cause.
When serum osmolality unavailable, use calculated osmolality = 2[Na] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8.

t.b: Quantifies hyponatraemia severity; <125 mmol/L = severe, 125‑129 mmol/L = moderate, 130‑134 mmol/L = mild.
Distinguishes hypotonic from isotonic or hypertonic hyponatraemia; <275 mOsm/kg confirms true hyponatraemia.
Answers whether kidneys can dilute urine; >100 mOsm/kg suggests ADH activity, <100 mOsm/kg indicates appropriate suppression.
Helps classify volume status; >30 mmol/L with euvolaemia points to SIADH, <30 mmol/L with hypovolaemia suggests extrarenal loss.

t.a: Serum cortisol (baseline) and ACTH stimulation test
t.b: Detects adrenal insufficiency; blunted cortisol rise after ACTH confirms primary or secondary failure.
Excludes hypothyroidism as a cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia.

t.a: Serum albumin and ascitic fluid analysis (if ascites present)
t.b: Calculate serum‑ascites albumin gradient; >1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension (cirrhosis) as hypervolemic cause.

t.a: Point‑of‑care urine dipstick for specific gravity
t.b: When formal osmolality unavailable, specific gravity >1.020 suggests concentrated urine, supporting ADH‑mediated hyponatraemia.

sections.p: Classification integrates serum sodium level, symptom burden and volume status to guide urgency of therapy.
b: Mild hyponatraemia: serum sodium 130‑134 mmol/L, asymptomatic or minimal nausea; treat with fluid restriction or address underlying cause.
Moderate hyponatraemia: serum sodium 125‑129 mmol/L, symptoms such as headache, confusion, mild seizures; initiate slower correction (≤8 mmol/L/24 h).
Acute hyponatraemia: onset <48 h, risk of cerebral oedema; correction may be faster (≤10 mmol/L/24 h) under ICU supervision.
Chronic hyponatraemia: onset >48 h, avoid rapid shifts; limit rise to ≤8 mmol/L/24 h to prevent osmotic demyelination.

Volume status classification: hypovolaemic (renal vs extrarenal loss), euvolaemic (SIADH, cerebral salt wasting, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), hypervolaemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).

sections.p: Certain disorders mimic hyponatraemia clinically or biochemically; systematic comparison avoids misdiagnosis.
b: Hypernatraemia in children – presents with irritability, fever, seizures; serum sodium >145 mmol/L, high serum osmolality, urine concentrating ability intact.

t.b: Occurs after SAH or brain trauma; euvolaemic or hypovolaemic, high urine sodium >30 mmol/L, polyuria, requires volume replacement – differentiate from SIADH by clinical hypovolaemia and falling haematocrit.
Seen with severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia; measured sodium low but serum osmolality normal; osmometer or direct ISE corrects value.

Elevated glucose draws water intracellularly; correct sodium = measured Na + 1.6 mmol/L for each 100 mg/dL glucose above 100; true hypotonic hyponatraemia persists if corrected Na remains <135 mmol/L.

sections.p: Treat hyponatraemia in a staged, patient‑centred way, balancing speed with safety. The ladder below guides initial actions, definitive therapy, monitoring and escalation.
b: 1. Immediate assessment of volume status and symptom severity
2. Stop any free‑water intake and correct underlying cause
3. Initiate fluid restriction (≤800 mL/day) if euvolemic or SIADH
4. Give hypertonic saline (3 % NaCl) for severe symptomatic cases
5. Add vasopressin receptor antagonist (vaptan) if fluid restriction fails
6. Consider demeclocycline or urea for chronic SIADH
7. Monitor serum sodium every 2–4 h during correction
8. Stop hypertonic saline when serum sodium rises 4–6 mmol/L in 24 h
9. Re‑evaluate for osmotic demyelination risk
10. Refer to neurology or ICU if seizures, coma or rapid correction risk

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key pharmacological agents used in hyponatraemia carry specific adverse effects and interactions that must be recognised and managed promptly.
b: Vaptans – risk of hyperkalaemia, liver injury; monitor liver enzymes and potassium
Hypertonic saline – risk of pulmonary oedema, arrhythmia; monitor vitals and chest X‑ray
Demeclocycline – nephrotoxicity, photosensitivity; avoid in renal impairment
Urea – GI upset, dehydration; ensure adequate fluid intake
Loop diuretics – hypokalaemia, volume depletion; correct potassium and volume
NSAIDs – worsen renal function; avoid in advanced CKD

t.b: Check serum potassium; give insulin‑glucose or calcium gluconate if >5.5 mmol/L
Stop vaptan; repeat LFTs in 48 h
Give diuretics, oxygen, and consider ICU monitoring
Discontinue demeclocycline; assess renal function
Replace potassium; consider potassium‑sparing diuretics

sections.p: Hyponatraemia can precipitate life‑threatening neurological and cardiovascular events; early recognition of complications dictates escalation.
b: Seizures – immediate 3 % NaCl and airway protection
Coma – urgent neurology/ICU referral
Rapid correction >10 mmol/L in 24 h – risk of osmotic demyelination; slow down
Pulmonary oedema – ICU admission
Re‑current hyponatraemia after correction – reassess cause and adjust therapy

t.b: Avoid rapid rise; aim 4–6 mmol/L in 24 h
Secure airway, give benzodiazepines, start hypertonic saline

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and external factors alter presentation, investigations and treatment of hyponatraemia.
b: HIV – opportunistic infections (TB, cryptococcal) can cause SIADH; monitor CD4
TB – adrenal involvement leads to adrenal crisis; check cortisol
Malnutrition – low albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure; adjust fluid restriction
Pregnancy – physiological dilution; avoid hypertonic saline unless severe
Diabetes – hyperglycaemia falsely lowers sodium; correct glucose first
Herbal remedies – some contain excess water or sodium; inquire
Alcohol – chronic use causes SIADH; treat withdrawal
Renal failure – restrict sodium and water; avoid nephrotoxic drugs
Liver failure – ascites alters volume assessment; use SAAG
Elderly – reduced thirst, altered drug metabolism; monitor closely

sections.p: Tailored approaches are required for children, pregnancy, the elderly, HIV patients and low‑resource settings.
b: Children – use isotonic saline for hypovolaemic cases; avoid hypertonic saline unless severe
Pregnancy – use 0.9 % saline; avoid high‑dose hypertonic solutions; monitor fetal wellbeing
Elderly – higher risk of osmotic demyelination; aim slower correction
HIV patients – screen for adrenal insufficiency; consider ART interactions
Low‑resource settings – use oral salt tablets or demeclocycline when IV access limited; rely on clinical assessment when labs unavailable

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside, investigations, management and complications.
b: 1. A 70‑year‑old with confusion and serum sodium 118 mmol/L – what is the first step?
2. How would you differentiate euvolemic from hypervolemic hyponatraemia on exam?
3. What serum osmolality threshold confirms hypotonic hyponatraemia?
4. Which drug is contraindicated in a patient with chronic kidney disease stage 4?
5. What is the maximum safe rise in serum sodium over 24 h to avoid osmotic demyelination?
6. In a patient with SIADH not responding to fluid restriction, which agent can be added?
7. What bedside sign indicates ascites and how is it performed?
8. How would you interpret a urine sodium of 60 mmol/L in a euvolemic patient?
9. What complication is most feared when correcting chronic hyponatraemia too rapidly?
10. In a pregnant woman with hyponatraemia, which fluid is preferred?

facts: Severe hyponatraemia: Na+ <125 mmol/L or seizures/coma
Mild hyponatraemia: Na+ 130‑134 mmol/L, usually asymptomatic
Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg suggests ADH activity (SIADH, CSW)
Urine Na+ >30 mmol/L in euvolaemic hyponatraemia points to SIADH
Correction limit: raise Na+ ≤8 mmol/L in 24 h, ≤12 mmol/L in 48 h
Fluid restriction 800‑1000 mL/day is first‑line for SIADH
Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) increase free water excretion in hypervolemic hyponatraemia

vivas.q: Define hyponatraemia and its clinical relevance in low‑resource settings.
vivas.a: Serum sodium <135 mmol/L; it predisposes to cerebral oedema, seizures and increased mortality, especially where monitoring is limited.

vivas.q: What bedside questions help determine volume status?
vivas.a: Ask about edema, orthostatic symptoms, recent fluid intake, vomiting/diarrhoea, diuretic use, heart failure symptoms, and recent infections.

vivas.q: Describe the physical exam sequence to assess volume status in hyponatraemia.
vivas.a: Inspect for edema, ascites, JVD; palpate peripheral pulses for thready vs bounding; measure blood pressure lying and standing; assess skin turgor; note lung crackles.

vivas.q: Why is rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia dangerous?
vivas.a: It creates an osmotic gradient causing brain cell dehydration and osmotic demyelination syndrome, presenting with quadriparesis, dysarthria, and locked‑in state.

vivas.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of 3% NaCl in severe symptomatic hyponatraemia?
vivas.a: It creates an extracellular hypertonic environment, pulling water out of brain cells and raising serum sodium rapidly.

vivas.q: A patient develops mild hyponatraemia after major surgery; which principle guides its correction?
vivas.a: Treat the underlying cause and avoid over‑correction; fluid restriction and careful monitoring are key.

vivas.q: Which crystalloid is least appropriate for maintenance in CKD stage 4 with vomiting‑induced hyponatraemia?
vivas.a: 0.9% normal saline, because its high chloride load can worsen acidosis and does not address free‑water excess.

vivas.q: What serious complication can occur if hypertonic saline is given too fast in chronic hyponatraemia?
vivas.a: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, presenting with delayed neurologic deficits after initial improvement.

vivas.q: Explain why a blunted ACTH stimulation test indicates primary adrenal insufficiency in hyponatraemia.
vivas.a: A blunted rise in cortisol after synthetic ACTH shows adrenal cortex failure; ACTH is high, confirming primary disease.

vivas.q: How does pregnancy alter the approach to hyponatraemia?
vivas.a: Physiologic plasma volume expansion and ADH increase; avoid hypertonic saline, use isotonic fluids, and monitor fetal status.

vivas.q: What are the three main clinical states of hyponatraemia based on volume and sodium?
vivas.a: Hypovolaemic (loss of Na+ and water), euvolaemic (SIADH, CSW), hypervolaemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).

vivas.q: Describe the key bedside test that cannot differentiate SIADH from CSW.
vivas.a: Urine sodium concentration; both can be >30 mmol/L, so urine Na alone cannot distinguish them.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line drug to add when fluid restriction fails in SIADH?
vivas.a: A vasopressin‑2 receptor antagonist (e.g., tolvaptan) if available; otherwise loop diuretic with salt tablets.

vivas.q: How do you manage severe hyponatraemia in a patient with acute liver failure where hypertonic saline is contraindicated?
vivas.a: Use cautious isotonic saline, consider albumin infusion, and correct underlying portal hypertension; avoid rapid shifts.

vivas.q: What are the red‑flag features that mandate urgent specialist referral?
vivas.a: Seizures, coma, Na+ <110 mmol/L, rapid fall >10 mmol/L in 24 h, osmotic demyelination risk, pregnancy, severe liver disease.

vivas.q: Why is demeclocycline rarely used in low‑resource settings for SIADH?
vivas.a: It requires monitoring for nephrotoxicity and has delayed onset; cheaper options like fluid restriction are preferred.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old man with heart failure presents with Na+ 122 mmol/L, edema, and JVD. Which management step is most appropriate?
o: Add furosemide and restrict free water
mcqs.e: Loop diuretic removes excess water and improves hyponatraemia in hypervolemic states.

mcqs.q: A postoperative patient has Na+ 132 mmol/L, urine osmolality 300 mOsm/kg, and is asymptomatic. What principle guides correction?
mcqs.e: Mild hyponatraemia without symptoms is managed conservatively with fluid restriction.

mcqs.q: Which adjunctive drug helps reduce high output ileostomy losses causing hyponatraemia?
mcqs.e: Octreotide reduces gastrointestinal secretions and output.

mcqs.q: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency presents with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. The hyperkalaemia is mainly due to:
mcqs.e: Lack of aldosterone impairs potassium excretion, causing hyperkalaemia.

mcqs.q: Which sign cannot be reliably assessed at the bedside to differentiate euvolaemic from hypervolaemic hyponatraemia?
mcqs.e: Urine specific gravity requires lab equipment, not a bedside physical sign.

cases.v: 45‑year‑old woman, HIV positive, on cotrimoxazole, presents with nausea, headache, Na+ 118 mmol/L, urine Na+ 45 mmol/L, urine osmolality 350 mOsm/kg, euvolaemic.

qs.q: What is the most likely aetiology?
qs.a: SIADH secondary to pulmonary infection or drug effect.
Fluid restriction to ≤800 mL/day and monitor serum Na+ every 4‑6 h.

qs.q: If Na+ does not rise after 24 h, which drug can be added?
qs.a: A vasopressin‑2 receptor antagonist (e.g., tolvaptan) if available.

cases.v: 68‑year‑old man with chronic heart failure, peripheral oedema, ascites, Na+ 124 mmol/L, urine Na+ 20 mmol/L, urine osmolality 500 mOsm/kg.

qs.a: Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia due to heart failure.
Increase loop diuretic dose and restrict free water intake.

qs.q: When should hypertonic saline be considered?
qs.a: Only if he becomes acutely symptomatic (seizures/coma) despite diuresis.

mistakes: Confusing SIADH with cerebral salt wasting; CSW needs volume replacement, SIADH needs restriction.
Using normal saline in hypervolemic hyponatraemia, which worsens fluid overload.
Correcting serum sodium >8 mmol/L in 24 h, risking osmotic demyelination.
Relying solely on urine sodium to diagnose SIADH without assessing volume status.
Failing to adjust fluid restriction for patients on diuretics or with high insensible losses.
Prescribing demeclocycline without monitoring renal function, especially in low‑resource settings.
Neglecting to check serum osmolality when sodium is low, missing pseudohyponatraemia.
Over‑looking drug‑induced hyponatraemia (e.g., SSRIs, carbamazepine) in the history.
